area: Area VII. Slow Flight and Stalls
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain what causes a spin, name its phases, say the spin recovery steps from memory, and spot the situations that lead to an accidental spin.
why: Loss of control in flight is the leading cause of fatal general aviation accidents, and half of the maneuvering-phase fatal accidents involve stall/spin. A spin needs a stall plus yaw, so a pilot who knows the traps can avoid most of them.

prereading.what: Spin awareness, the four spin phases, the six-step spin recovery template, intentional spins, weight and balance, common errors, spiral dive.
prereading.label: AFH 5-22 to 5-26

prereading.what: Stall/spin definitions, factors that change stall speed, distractions, stall recognition, primary cause of spins, spin recovery.
prereading.label: AC 61-67C, Ch 1 (para 100 to 112)

prereading.what: Stall recognition cues, when the published stall speed is valid, AOA indicators and their limits.
prereading.label: AFH 5-13 to 5-14

prereading.what: Critical AOA, stalls in turns, the stall speed and load factor chart.
prereading.label: PHAK 5-25 to 5-26

prereading.what: How normal, utility and acrobatic airplanes are spin tested, and spin placards.
prereading.label: AC 61-67C, Ch 4 (para 400 to 402)

warmup: Your trainer has a placard that says no spins are approved. Does that mean it can't spin? What would have to happen for it to spin anyway?

key_terms.def: An aggravated stall that leads to autorotation: the airplane follows a downward corkscrew path.
Self-sustaining rotation. The rising wing is less stalled than the descending wing, so the roll keeps going.
The angle of attack where the wing stalls. Same angle at any airspeed, weight or load factor.
Lift divided by weight, in G. More G means a higher stall speed.
From the stall and start of rotation until the spin is fully developed.
Rotation rate, airspeed and descent rate are steady; the spin is in balance.
A steep, descending, tightening turn. The wing is NOT stalled, so airspeed and G build fast.
A new stall caused by pulling back too hard or too soon during a recovery.
A stall with aileron one way and rudder the other, such as a skidding base-to-final turn.
Loss of control in flight: a big, unintended departure from the planned flightpath.

body.p: A spin is an aggravated stall that ends in autorotation. The airplane follows a downward corkscrew path [[24:127|AFH 5-22]]. In every spin at least one wing is stalled [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].

Two things are needed: a stall, and yaw. A spin starts when at least one wing passes the critical AOA while sideslip or yaw is acting on the airplane at or beyond the stall [[24:127|AFH 5-22]]. No stall, no spin [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].
Why does it keep turning? As the airplane rotates, the rising wing is less stalled than the descending wing. That makes it roll, yaw and pitch down in a spiral path [[13:11|AC 61-67C para 107]].

callout.text: Stall + yaw = spin. Take away either one and there is no spin.

body.p: Where the yaw comes from [[24:127|AFH 5-22]]:

bullets: Wrong rudder use (too much or too little).
Adverse yaw from aileron.
Engine and prop effects: P-factor, torque, spiraling slipstream, gyroscopic precession.
Wind shear, including wake turbulence.

callout.text: Modern airplanes are more reluctant to spin than older designs, but it is not impossible. Mishandled turns, stalls and uncoordinated slow flight can spin even reluctant airplanes [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].

check.q: What two things must happen for an airplane to enter a spin?
check.a: The wing must be stalled (past the critical AOA) and the airplane must be yawing [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].

body.p: A stall happens when the wing passes its critical AOA. It can happen at any airspeed, in any attitude, at any power setting [[13:7|AC 61-67C para 100]]. The stall comes from too much AOA, not from too little airspeed [[13:7|AC 61-67C para 100]].
Each airplane stalls at the same AOA no matter the airspeed, weight, load factor or density altitude. The critical AOA is about 16° to 20°, depending on the design [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]].

Load factor raises stall speed. Stall speed goes up with the square root of the load factor [[13:8|AC 61-67C para 100g]]. Bank angle raises load factor fast once you pass about 45° to 50° [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]].

head: Situation
Load factor
Effect on stall
rows: Stall speed about 40% higher [[13:7|AC 61-67C para 100b]] (AFH says 41% [[24:114|AFH 5-9]])
A 45-knot stall speed becomes 90 knots [[13:8|AC 61-67C para 100g]]

body.p: Danger zone: in a steep turn the nose drops, and the pilot pulls back without shallowing the bank. That tightens the turn and can lead to a diving spiral [[13:8|AC 61-67C para 100g]]. A stall above 1 G is an accelerated stall. It comes at a higher-than-normal airspeed [[24:124|AFH 5-19]] and can surprise an inexperienced pilot [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

callout.text: The published stall speed is only good in unaccelerated 1G flight, coordinated (ball centered), at one weight and one CG [[24:118|AFH 5-13]]. Change any of these and the stall speed changes.

check.q: Your airplane stalls at 45 knots in level flight. Can it stall at 90 knots?
check.a: Yes. At 4 G a 45-knot stall speed becomes 90 knots [[13:8|AC 61-67C para 100g]].

chunks.title: Power, weight, CG, configuration and yaw

body.p: The kind of spin an airplane gets depends on its design, loading, control inputs and density altitude [[24:127|AFH 5-22]]. Here is how each factor matters:

head: Factor
What it does
Source
rows: Power makes a spin worse. It can flatten the spin and usually speeds up rotation.
High power, low speed, high pitch
P-factor yaws the airplane left. Wrong rudder correction = uncoordinated flight. Classic case: go-around or short-field takeoff.
More weight = higher stall speed, because the wing needs more AOA for more lift.
Less elevator force needed to stall, so accidental stalls are easier. Extreme aft CG can cause a flat spin; recovery from a flat spin is often impossible.
Stalls at a higher airspeed; needs more back-elevator force.
Flaps generally lower stall speed (white arc starts below green arc).
If extended before the spin, retract them as soon as practicable after spin entry.
A stall can happen in any attitude, so the nose position alone won't tell you.

body.p: Small loading changes matter. An airplane that cleanly recovers from a long spin at one CG may not respond to normal recovery inputs when the CG moves aft by one or two inches [[1:140|PHAK 5-43]]. A flat spin is when centrifugal force, acting through a CG far aft, pulls the tail out away from the spin axis, so the nose can't be lowered to recover [[1:141|PHAK 5-44]].

callout.text: An airplane approved for spins in the utility category, but loaded for the normal category, may not recover from a spin that goes beyond one turn [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]. A suitcase in the aft baggage compartment can be enough to change spin behavior [[13:12|AC 61-67C para 108]].

body.p: Which way will it spin? A spin from cross-controlling usually rotates the way the rudder is pushed, no matter which wingtip is up [[13:12|AC 61-67C para 109]]. In a skidding turn it spins the way the controls are applied. In a slipping turn it usually spins opposite the aileron being held [[13:12|AC 61-67C para 109]].

check.q: Why is an aft CG dangerous for spins?
check.a: It takes less elevator force to stall, so stalls come easier, and an extreme aft CG can lead to a flat spin that may not be recoverable [[13:9|AC 61-67C para 100h]].

chunks.title: The four phases of a spin

body.p: A spin has four phases: entry, incipient, developed and recovery [[24:128|AFH 5-23]].

head: Phase
What is happening
How to recognize it
rows: The pilot, on purpose or by accident, provides the stall and the yaw.
Stall with yaw or uncoordinated controls [[24:129|AFH 5-24]]
From the stall and start of rotation until the spin is fully developed. May take 2 to 4 turns in most airplanes.
Airspeed settles low and steady; turn indicator shows spin direction [[24:129|AFH 5-24]]
Rotation rate, airspeed and vertical speed are stable; path is nearly vertical. The spin is in balance.
Rotation stops and AOA drops below critical. Can take a quarter turn up to several turns.

callout.text: Don't use the ball to tell spin direction. The ball moves based on where it is mounted, not the spin. Use the turn indicator (symbolic airplane) instead [[24:129|AFH 5-24]].

body.p: Start recovery early. Begin incipient spin recovery before 360° of rotation [[24:129|AFH 5-24]].

How much altitude? The first turn loses about 1,000 feet; each turn after that loses about half that much [[24:128|AFH 5-23]]. Another rough estimate: about 500 feet per 3-second turn in most small airplanes approved for spins, with more loss at higher density altitude [[13:13|AC 61-67C para 111]].

Spin or spiral? Some trainers won't reach the developed phase and may slide from the incipient phase into a spiral dive. A spiral is not in balance: it keeps accelerating and G load can build fast [[24:129|AFH 5-24]]. In a real spin, airspeed normally stays below stall speed; a rapidly increasing airspeed means a spiral [[13:19|AC 61-67C para 300f]] [[13:20|AC 61-67C para 300f]].

check.q: Airspeed is climbing fast while you are turning nose-down. Spin or spiral?
check.a: Spiral. In a spin the airplane is stalled and airspeed stays low and steady; increasing airspeed means you are no longer in a spin [[24:130|AFH 5-25]].

chunks.title: Fly it step by step: spin recovery

callout.text: Always use the manufacturer's (POH/AFM) spin recovery. Use the generic steps below only if the POH has none [[24:129|AFH 5-24]] [[24:130|AFH 5-25]].

body.p: The six steps, and why [[24:129|AFH 5-24]] [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]:

bullets: 1. Power to idle. Power makes the spin flatter and usually faster.
2. Ailerons neutral. Aileron with the spin can speed up rotation; aileron against it can flatten the spin or even make it unrecoverable.
3. Full opposite rudder, briskly, and hold it until rotation stops. Rudder is usually the most important control. Slow, timid rudder can let the airplane keep spinning.
4. Brisk, straight forward elevator (forward of neutral), right after the rudder. Don't wait for rotation to stop. Some airplanes need full forward elevator.
5. Neutralize rudder when rotation stops, or you will yaw or sideslip as speed builds.
6. Back elevator to return to level flight, and adjust power. Don't pull too hard: that can cause a secondary stall and another spin. Stay within G and airspeed limits.

callout.text: PARE (a common flight-school memory aid for steps 1 to 4): Power idle, Ailerons neutral, Rudder opposite, Elevator forward. Then neutralize rudder and pull out gently.

body.p: Extra points from AC 61-67C [[13:13|AC 61-67C para 111]]:

bullets: The engine may quit in a spin because fuel slosh interrupts flow, so assume power is not available.
Neutralize the rudder when spinning stops, to avoid a spin the other way.
Too much or too abrupt back elevator during the pullout can cause a secondary stall and possibly another spin.

body.p: This Task has only Knowledge and Risk Management elements and no Skills elements (ACS PA.VII.D), so there are no flight tolerances. The examiner will ask you to explain the recovery and the risks. Private pilot training does not include practicing spins; it stresses stall and spin avoidance [[13:15|AC 61-67C para 200]].

check.q: Should you wait for rotation to stop before moving the elevator forward?
check.a: No. Apply brisk forward elevator right after full opposite rudder; don't wait for rotation to stop [[24:130|AFH 5-25]].

chunks.title: Common errors and the spiral trap

body.p: Common recovery errors [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]:

bullets: Not applying full rudder (to the stops) briskly against the spin.
Not enough forward elevator.
Waiting for rotation to stop before applying forward elevator.
Not neutralizing the rudder after rotation stops (possible secondary spin).
Slow, overly cautious control movements.
Too much back elevator after rotation stops (secondary stall).
Too little back elevator in the pullout (too much airspeed).

body.p: A spiral dive needs a different fix. It is a nose-low, tightening turn where the wing is NOT stalled, so speed and G build fast [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]. The startled pilot may yank back while rolling level, which can damage or break the airplane [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].

head: Spin
Spiral dive
rows: Power idle, ailerons neutral, opposite rudder, forward elevator [[24:129|AFH 5-24]]
Power idle, small push to unload, roll wings level (coordinated), gently raise nose, then climb power [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]

callout.text: Opposite rudder and forward elevator are for a spin. In a spiral, the key is to unload, roll level, then gently raise the nose. Read the airspeed first.

check.q: Name two control errors that can cause a secondary stall or spin after rotation stops.
check.a: Not neutralizing the rudder (secondary spin) and too much back elevator (secondary stall) [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].

body.p: Loss of control in flight (LOC-I) is the leading cause of fatal GA accidents, and maneuvering is the most common phase for it [[24:106|AFH 5-1]]. More than 25 percent of GA fatal accidents happen while maneuvering, and half of those involve stall/spin [[1:123|PHAK 5-26]].
The primary cause of an accidental spin: going past the critical AOA with too much or too little rudder and, to a lesser extent, aileron [[13:12|AC 61-67C para 109]].

head: Trap
What happens
rows: Tailwind on base causes an overshoot. Pilot adds bank, back pressure and inside rudder; bank steepens, nose drops, pilot pulls; the airplane can snap into a spin. Go around instead [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].
High pitch, high power, low speed: P-factor yaw plus poor rudder control [[13:12|AC 61-67C para 109]]. Nose-high trim or early flap retraction during go-arounds [[13:11|AC 61-67C para 104b]].
Full power with nose-up approach trim makes the nose rise sharply and turn left [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].
Pulling without shallowing the bank tightens the turn and can lead to a diving spiral [[13:8|AC 61-67C para 100g]].
Unnecessary low flying and impromptu demonstrations can push pilots past their abilities [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].

callout.text: In the pattern, be reluctant to bank more than 30°, and never skid the turn to fix an overshoot [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

body.p: Distractions are when it happens. Stalls from poor airspeed control are most likely when the pilot is busy with something else: a checklist, an engine restart, a windy pattern, a chart or fuel math, or reaching for something on the floor or in the back seat [[13:9|AC 61-67C para 101]]. Setting avionics can also pull attention away from flying [[24:107|AFH 5-2]].

Losing the horizon matters too. Continuing VFR into marginal VMC or IMC raises the chance of spatial disorientation and upset [[24:107|AFH 5-2]]. From 2008 to 2013 nearly 200 accidents were tied to spatial disorientation, and more than 70% were fatal [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].

callout.text: Placarded against spins? Normal category airplanes certified under the old 14 CFR 23.221(a) only had to recover from a one-turn or 3-second spin (whichever takes longer) within one more turn, or show spin resistance. There is no assurance of recovery from a fully developed spin; assume the airplane could become uncontrollable [[24:130|AFH 5-25]].

check.q: You overshoot final on a gusty day. What is the safest action?
check.a: Go around. Don't steepen the bank past about 30° or skid the turn with inside rudder [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

chunks.title: Stall warnings: what they do and don't tell you

body.p: Many airplanes have stall warning devices that alert you 4 to 8 knots before the stall [[13:10|AC 61-67C para 103]]. Other warning signs: mushy controls, a loss of rpm in fixed-pitch airplanes with power on, less wind noise, and buffet or vibration just before the stall [[13:10|AC 61-67C para 103]].

head: Cue
Limitation
rows: Most vintage airplanes, and many light-sport and experimental ones, have none; certification allows warning by buffet alone [[24:118|AFH 5-13]]. The system can fail, so use other cues [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].
With ice or other wing contamination, the stall can come with little or none of the usual cues, including buffet and the horn [[13:10|AC 61-67C para 102a]].
Stall speed changes with G, weight, CG and coordination [[24:118|AFH 5-13]]. In uncoordinated flight the airspeed and altimeter are unreliable [[13:12|AC 61-67C para 109]].
Not foolproof, since you can stall in any attitude [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].
It can mask the feel of a stall; a sudden disconnect with odd trim can lead to a spin or spiral [[13:10|AC 61-67C para 102c]].
Shows margin to critical AOA, but limited by calibration, unheated probes, indicator type, flap setting and wing contamination [[24:118|AFH 5-13]] [[24:119|AFH 5-14]].

callout.text: In a skidding cross-control stall, the warning can be very short. This stall can occur with very little warning and can be deadly close to the ground [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

body.p: React at the first warning. Reduce the AOA first (lower the nose), then roll wings level and add power as needed [[24:120|AFH 5-15]] [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. AC 61-67C also lists adding power, lowering the nose and reducing the bank [[13:10|AC 61-67C para 103]], but the newer AFH stresses that reducing AOA comes first. Don't disable a required stall warning device for a checkride [[13:22|AC 61-67C para 402]].

check.q: Why can't you count on the stall horn when the wing has frost or ice?
check.a: Contamination can cause a stall with little or none of the usual cues, including the horn and buffet, and can raise stall speed [[13:10|AC 61-67C para 102a]].

body.p: Turbulence: a vertical gust or wind shear can suddenly raise the AOA and cause a stall at a much higher airspeed than normal, often while you fight for control on a gusty approach [[13:9|AC 61-67C para 100l]]. In moderate to severe turbulence or strong crosswinds, fly a higher-than-normal approach speed [[13:9|AC 61-67C para 100l]].

Microbursts: a headwind that turns to a tailwind drops airspeed and performance [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]]. A microburst can make downdrafts up to 6,000 fpm and headwind losses of 30 to 90 knots [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]].

Density altitude: altitude has little or no effect on indicated stall speed, so fly the normal indicated speeds [[13:9|AC 61-67C para 100j]]. But expect bigger altitude loss in a spin at higher density altitude [[13:13|AC 61-67C para 111]], and a normally aspirated engine makes less power as altitude increases [[13:15|AC 61-67C para 200]].
Ice and frost: even a small amount raises stall speed. Don't fly with snow, ice or frost on the airplane [[13:9|AC 61-67C para 100k]].

Collision hazards: you will be looking down and inside during stall work, so clear first. Clear the area above and below before slowing for a spin [[24:128|AFH 5-23]], and use clearing turns before any training maneuver [[24:33|AFH 1-12]].

bullets: Most midair collisions happen in good VFR, in daylight, within 5 miles of an airport [[24:31|AFH 1-10]].
Scan in short steps of no more than 10 degrees, at least 1 second each [[24:32|AFH 1-11]].
An airplane with no relative motion that keeps getting bigger is on a collision course: act now [[24:32|AFH 1-11]].

callout.text: Practice stalls high enough to recover at least 1,500 feet AGL in a single-engine airplane [[13:10|AC 61-67C para 103]].

check.q: Does high density altitude change your indicated stall speed?
check.a: Little or none, so fly normal indicated speeds; but spin altitude loss is greater at high density altitude [[13:9|AC 61-67C para 100j]] [[13:13|AC 61-67C para 111]].

scenario.title: Gusty base turn with a passenger
scenario.setup: You are a new private pilot with a friend aboard, landing on a warm, gusty afternoon. There is a tailwind on base that you didn't notice. Your friend asks you to point out their house just as you start the turn to final. You realize you are overshooting the centerline.

questions.q: What is happening, and what is the tempting but dangerous fix?
questions.a: The tailwind on base raised groundspeed, so you turned late and overshot. The tempting fix is more bank, more back pressure and inside rudder to swing the nose around. That is a skidding cross-control setup that can stall and spin with little warning [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

Go around. In the pattern, be reluctant to bank more than 30° and never skid the turn to fix an overshoot [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]. On the go-around, hold the nose down against the nose-up trim and use right rudder for P-factor [[24:126|AFH 5-21]] [[13:12|AC 61-67C para 109]].

questions.q: How did the passenger and the gusts add risk?
questions.a: The question was a distraction at a busy, low-speed moment, which is when airspeed-control stalls are most likely [[13:9|AC 61-67C para 101]]. Gusts can suddenly raise the AOA and stall the wing at a higher airspeed, so fly a higher-than-normal approach speed [[13:9|AC 61-67C para 100l]]. Tell passengers before the flight that you can't talk in the pattern.

questions.q: If the airplane did start to rotate, what would you do, and why is altitude the real problem?
questions.a: Follow the POH spin recovery; if none, power idle, ailerons neutral, full opposite rudder, brisk forward elevator, neutralize rudder when rotation stops, then pull out gently [[24:129|AFH 5-24]] [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]. The first spin turn loses about 1,000 feet [[24:128|AFH 5-23]], more than a typical pattern gives you, so prevention is the only real defense.

quiz.q: Which TWO conditions must exist for a spin?
options: High airspeed and steep bank
A stalled wing and yaw
Full flaps and high power
Aft CG and turbulence
quiz.why: A spin needs at least one wing past the critical AOA with yaw or sideslip acting on the airplane [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].

quiz.q: In a level, coordinated 60° bank turn, the load factor is:
options: 2 G
3 G
4 G
quiz.why: A 60° banked level turn produces 2 G, and stall speed rises about 40% [[13:7|AC 61-67C para 100b]].

quiz.q: With no POH procedure, what is the FIRST spin recovery step?
options: Full forward elevator
Ailerons opposite the spin
Power (throttle) to idle
Full opposite rudder
quiz.why: Step 1 is power to idle; power flattens the spin and usually speeds rotation [[24:129|AFH 5-24]].

quiz.q: When should forward elevator be applied in spin recovery?
options: After rotation stops
Right after full opposite rudder
Before reducing power
Only if airspeed is increasing
quiz.why: Apply brisk forward elevator immediately after full rudder; don't wait for rotation to stop [[24:130|AFH 5-25]].

quiz.q: Which instrument should NOT be used to find the spin direction?
options: Turn indicator
Turn coordinator symbolic airplane
Slip/skid ball
Outside view
quiz.why: The ball's movement depends on where it is mounted, not on the spin direction [[24:129|AFH 5-24]].

quiz.q: During a nose-low rotation the airspeed is rapidly increasing. You are most likely in:
options: A developed spin
An incipient spin
A flat spin
A spiral dive
quiz.why: In a spin the wing is stalled and airspeed is low and steady; increasing airspeed means a spiral [[24:130|AFH 5-25]] [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].

quiz.q: Many stall warning devices alert the pilot about how far before the stall?
options: 1 to 2 knots
4 to 8 knots
10 to 15 knots
20 knots
quiz.why: Many stall warning devices alert 4 to 8 knots before the stall [[13:10|AC 61-67C para 103]].

quiz.q: A classic stall/spin accident in the pattern comes from:
options: A shallow, coordinated base-to-final turn
A skidding base-to-final turn to fix an overshoot
A stabilized approach at the normal speed
A slip to lose altitude with wings level
quiz.why: Overshooting final and using inside rudder to skid the nose around can stall and spin the airplane; go around instead [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

takeaways: No stall, no spin: a spin needs a stalled wing plus yaw.
The wing can stall at any airspeed, attitude or power; G, weight and CG move the stall speed.
Recovery (if no POH procedure): power idle, ailerons neutral, full opposite rudder, brisk forward elevator, neutralize rudder, gentle pullout.
Rising airspeed means a spiral, not a spin: unload, roll level, then raise the nose.
Stall warnings can be late, missing or masked; react to the first cue.
Biggest traps: skidding base-to-final turns, go-arounds, distractions and gusts. When in doubt, go around.
cfi_notes: This Task has no Skills elements; it is tested orally. Tie it to PA.VII.A to C stall demos and slow flight with realistic distractions (AC 61-67C para 200a lists examples like dropping a pencil or reading a chart) [[13:16|AC 61-67C para 200]].
Students often think stalls are about airspeed. Keep saying 'angle of attack' and show Figure 5-39 for G.
PARE is a popular memory aid but is not in the FAA texts; teach it as matching AFH Figure 5-17 steps 1 to 4, and stress the POH comes first.

Note the numbers differ by source: AFH text says incipient may take 2 to 4 turns, while AFH Figure 5-16 shows about 2 turns in 4 to 6 seconds; altitude loss is about 1,000 ft for the first turn (AFH text) vs about 500 ft per 3-second turn (AC 61-67C and Figure 5-16). Present them as rough estimates.
Examiners probe: spin vs spiral, why ailerons stay neutral, why the ball is unreliable in a spin, how aft CG affects recovery, and what the 'no spins' placard means.
Students may wrongly use spin recovery inputs in a spiral (or the reverse). Drill: check airspeed first.

Under 14 CFR 91.307(c), a pilot carrying anyone other than a crewmember may not intentionally exceed 60° of bank or 30° nose-up or nose-down unless every occupant wears an approved parachute. Exceptions (91.307(d)): pilot certification flight tests, and spins and other maneuvers required for a certificate or rating when given by a CFI or an ATP instructing under 61.67 [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307]]. Spin training is required only for flight instructor airplane/glider applicants [[13:19|AC 61-67C para 300]] [[60:339|14 CFR 61.183(i)]].
gaps: The make-and-model spin recovery procedure, whether the airplane is approved for spins, and its spin/utility category loading limits come from the POH/AFM and placards, not these sources.
The acronym 'PARE' does not appear in the AFH, AC 61-67C or PHAK; the lesson labels it as a flight-school memory aid for the AFH six-step template.
The ACS Task has no Skills elements, so there are no tolerances to list.
AC 61-67C and the AFH don't give a microburst-specific spin discussion; the microburst content comes from PHAK Ch 12 general wind shear guidance.

activities.title: True or false: what makes a spin

cards.s: If the wing never stalls, the airplane cannot spin.
cards.why: Yes. In every spin at least one wing is stalled. No stall, no spin [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].

cards.s: A wing can only stall when the airspeed is low.
cards.why: No. A stall comes from too much AOA, not too little airspeed. It can happen at any airspeed, in any attitude, at any power setting [[13:7|AC 61-67C para 100b]].

cards.s: Modern trainers can't spin; only older designs can.
cards.why: No. Modern airplanes are more reluctant to spin, but it is not impossible. Mishandled turns, stalls and uncoordinated slow flight can still spin them [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].

cards.s: Adding weight to the airplane raises its stall speed.
cards.why: Yes. More weight needs more lift, so the wing needs a higher AOA, and the stall speed goes up [[13:9|AC 61-67C para 100i]].

cards.s: Keeping the power in during a spin helps you fly out of it.
cards.why: No. Power makes a spin worse. It can flatten the spin and usually speeds up the rotation, so step 1 is power to idle [[24:129|AFH 5-24]].

cards.s: Adverse yaw from the ailerons can supply the yaw that starts a spin.
cards.why: Yes. Yaw can come from rudder misuse, adverse yaw from aileron, engine and prop effects, or wind shear [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].

final_quiz.q: Your airplane stalls at 48 knots in straight and level flight. You pull up hard and put 4 G on the wings. About what airspeed could it stall at now?
options: 48 knots
68 knots
96 knots
192 knots
final_quiz.why: Stall speed goes up with the square root of the load factor. The square root of 4 is 2, so 48 x 2 = 96 knots [[13:8|AC 61-67C para 100g]]. Multiplying by 4 (192) is the common mistake.

final_quiz.q: You load heavy bags in the aft baggage area. The CG is still in limits, but near the aft limit. Compared with a forward CG, what should you expect?
options: Less back-elevator force is needed to stall, so an accidental stall is easier
A higher stall speed and heavier elevator forces
No change in spin behavior, since the CG is within limits
The airplane can no longer spin at all
final_quiz.why: As the CG moves aft, it takes less elevator force to reach a high AOA, so accidental stalls come easier [[13:8|AC 61-67C para 100h]]. Even a change within limits can seriously affect spin recovery [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]. A higher stall speed with heavier forces describes a forward CG [[13:9|AC 61-67C para 100h]].

final_quiz.q: You are in a slipping turn, holding left aileron against right rudder, when the wing stalls. Which way will the spin most likely go?
options: Left, the way the aileron is held
Right, the way the rudder is pushed
Toward whichever wing is lower at the stall
It can't spin, because the controls cancel out
final_quiz.why: A cross-control spin usually rotates the way the rudder is applied, no matter which wingtip is up. In a slip, that is opposite the aileron being held [[13:12|AC 61-67C para 109]] [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].

final_quiz.q: Use the AFH rule of thumb: the first spin turn loses about 1,000 feet and each turn after that loses about half as much. About how much altitude do 4 full turns use?
options: About 500 feet
About 1,000 feet
About 4,000 feet
About 2,500 feet
final_quiz.why: 1,000 feet for the first turn plus 3 x 500 feet for the next three = 2,500 feet [[24:128|AFH 5-23]]. That is why even a short spin near the ground is so dangerous.

final_quiz.q: During spin recovery, why should the ailerons be held neutral?
options: Ailerons are the main control that stops the rotation
Aileron against the spin can flatten it and may even make it unrecoverable
Aileron against the spin is needed to level the wings first
Ailerons have no effect at all in a spin
final_quiz.why: Aileron with the spin can speed up rotation, and aileron against the spin can flatten it, delay recovery, or even cause an unrecoverable spin. Neutral is best [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]. Rudder, not aileron, is usually the most important control [[24:130|AFH 5-25]].

final_quiz.q: In a spin recovery, the rotation has just stopped and airspeed is starting to build. You are still holding full opposite rudder and forward elevator. What comes next?
options: Neutralize the rudder, then gently raise the nose to level flight
Pull back hard right away to stop the altitude loss
Keep holding the rudder until you reach cruise speed
Add full power before doing anything else
final_quiz.why: Neutralize the rudder when rotation stops, or you will yaw or sideslip as speed builds. Then use back elevator to return to level flight, without pulling too hard, which can cause a secondary stall and another spin [[24:130|AFH 5-25]].

final_quiz.q: You fly into a cloud by mistake. Soon you see a steep bank and a low nose, and the airspeed and wind noise are rising fast. What should you do first?
options: Apply full opposite rudder and brisk forward elevator
Pull back firmly while rolling the wings level
Reduce power to idle, then push a little to unload before rolling level
Add full power and pull up to climb out of the cloud
final_quiz.why: Rising airspeed means a spiral dive, not a spin, because the wing is not stalled. Recovery: power idle, a small push to unload, roll wings level, then gently raise the nose. Pulling back while rolling level can overstress or break the airplane [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].

final_quiz.q: You are on final with the trim set nose-up for the approach glide. You decide to go around and add full power. What should you expect and do?
options: The nose rises sharply and turns left; push forward, use right rudder, and retrim
The nose drops; pull back hard to hold altitude
Nothing changes, because the trim adjusts itself to the power
The nose rises and turns right; use left rudder
final_quiz.why: Propwash plus nose-up trim make the nose rise sharply and turn left, so hold forward pressure and retrim [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]. Right rudder counters the left yaw from P-factor at high power and low speed [[13:12|AC 61-67C para 109]].

final_quiz.q: On downwind, your passenger drops a phone between the seats and asks you to help find it. What is the best choice?
options: Trim nose-up and reach for it quickly
Keep flying the airplane and leave the phone for after landing
Slow down so you have more time to search
Have the passenger hold the yoke while you look
final_quiz.why: Stalls from poor airspeed control are most likely when the pilot is busy with something else, such as a windy pattern or reaching for items on the floor or back seat [[13:9|AC 61-67C para 101]]. Fly the airplane first.

final_quiz.q: Your trainer has a placard that says no acrobatic maneuvers, including spins, are approved. What does that tell you?
options: The airplane is built so that it cannot spin
Spins are fine as long as you keep them to one turn
Spins are allowed if a flight instructor is aboard
There is no assurance it will recover from a fully developed spin
final_quiz.why: In airplanes placarded against spins, there is no assurance of recovery from a fully developed spin, and the pilot should assume the airplane could become uncontrollable [[24:130|AFH 5-25]] [[13:22|AC 61-67C para 402]].

final_quiz.q: You rent an older airplane that has no stall horn or light. Which statement is true?
options: It is not airworthy until a stall horn is installed
It can't stall as long as you stay coordinated
Pitch attitude alone will always warn you of a stall
Certification can allow buffet alone as the warning, so watch for feel, sound and buffet
final_quiz.why: Most vintage airplanes have no stall warning device. Certification lets the manufacturer provide the warning through pre-stall buffet. Since you can stall in any attitude, vision is not foolproof [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].

final_quiz.q: You are landing on a day with moderate turbulence and a strong crosswind. Which approach speed is best?
options: Slower than normal, to shorten the landing roll
Exactly normal, since gusts don't affect the stall
A bit higher than normal, because a gust can suddenly raise the AOA
Normal, but cut the power early to stay above the gusts
final_quiz.why: A vertical gust or wind shear can abruptly raise the AOA and stall the wing at a much higher airspeed than normal. In moderate to severe turbulence or strong crosswinds, keep a higher-than-normal approach speed [[13:9|AC 61-67C para 100l]].

final_quiz.q: Before stall practice, you see another airplane ahead. It stays in the same spot on your windshield but keeps getting bigger. What does that mean?
options: It is moving away, so no action is needed
It is likely on a collision course; take evasive action now
It is flying the same direction at the same speed, so it is safe
It is far below you and will pass underneath
final_quiz.why: An aircraft with no relative motion is likely on a collision course. If it shows no sideways or up-down motion but keeps growing, take immediate evasive action [[24:32|AFH 1-11]].
